hints: Look closely at the pairing in DNA: every cytosine on one strand pairs with a guanine on the opposite strand, so think about what that means for the whole double helix.
Remember Chargaff's rule applies to the complete DNA molecule (%C = %G), but a single strand on its own does not have to have equal C and G.
walkthrough:
**Recall how C and G pair**

Think of DNA like a zip. A cytosine on one strand always forms 3 hydrogen bonds with a guanine on the other strand.

So every C in the whole molecule has a matching G partner:
$$\text{total C} = \text{total G}$$

**Whole molecule versus single strand**

For the whole double-stranded molecule, the percentages must match. That is Chargaff's rule.

But within just one strand, there is no rule that C must equal G. One strand could be C-rich and the other G-rich, and they would still pair perfectly.

**Pick the correct description**

Only the statement about the whole molecule having equal %C and %G is always true. That points straight to B.

options.A: Incorrect, because C pairs 1:1 with G across the two strands, so their percentages in the whole molecule are equal, not half.
options.B: Correct, because every C pairs with a G in the double helix, so %C = %G when you count both strands together.
options.C: Incorrect, because pairing is between strands, not within a strand, so a single strand can have very different amounts of C and G.
options.D: Incorrect, because the two strands are complementary, so if one strand is high in C the other will be high in G. The %C can differ between strands.
